questions.question: Where does the browser get celestial states at runtime — from the Express API over HTTP, or from the astronomy package bundled and executed in the browser? ADR-006 says "Normal rendering does not depend on a remote ephemeris API" and cites offline capability, while 001 §5 and §25 and all of Document 003 show React → Astronomy Client → HTTP/JSON → Express → astronomy package. These cannot both be true as written.
questions.why_it_matters: This decides whether the astronomy package must be browser-safe and bundled into apps/web, whether the API is on the critical path for time animation and orbit generation (and therefore needs the batch endpoint and caching much earlier), and what 'offline capability' means in the README. It also changes H016–H022 task scoping and the dependency graph in 005 §16.
options: Browser imports packages/astronomy directly; the Express API exists as a demonstrable, independently testable boundary and for CLI/tooling, but the app does not call it during normal rendering
Browser always calls the API; ADR-006 means only 'no third-party ephemeris service', and offline capability is dropped as a V1 claim
Hybrid: API is the source for the initial load and explicit date jumps; the client-side package handles continuous animation between fetches

questions.question: What exactly is the supported date range for V1, and what happens outside it? Six documents refer to a 'supported date range' and 002 §21 defines UnsupportedDateRangeError, but no bounds are ever stated. Schlyter's stated target is the 20th–21st centuries, and his Pluto formula is explicitly valid only 1800–2100.
questions.why_it_matters: It determines the validation rejection boundary in the API schema layer, the clamping behaviour of the simulation clock and timeline UI, which fixture dates the validation agents must generate, and what accuracy metadata (supportedDateRange) each model publishes. A guess here silently changes what the app will refuse to render.
options: 1900-01-01 to 2100-01-01 UTC, hard-rejected outside with UnsupportedDateRangeError (matches the tutorial's stated target and Pluto's validity window)
1800–2100, hard-rejected outside
A wider soft range (e.g. 1000–3000) that computes but returns degraded accuracy metadata / a warning flag, with a narrower validated range
Different ranges per model/body, declared in AccuracyMetadata and enforced per-body

questions.question: Do the frame identifiers HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC / GEOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC / GEOCENTRIC_EQUATORIAL denote the ecliptic and equinox *of date*, or J2000? 002 §9 lists them as stable identifiers and §16 requires precess(state, fromEpoch, toEpoch) with 'the supported model and validity range must be documented', but no precession model is named and no default equinox is stated. Schlyter's time-varying elements are referred to the ecliptic and mean equinox of date.
questions.why_it_matters: The equinox is part of the frame definition; without it a coordinate triple is as ambiguous as one with no frame at all — which is exactly what ADR-008 forbids. It also determines whether Horizons fixtures must be requested in mean-of-date or ICRF/J2000, and whether precession is needed at all for V1 or is deferred.
options: Frames are mean equinox and ecliptic of date; add explicit J2000-suffixed frame identifiers later when a precession model is implemented
Frames are J2000; the Schlyter output is precessed from of-date to J2000 inside the model, using a named precession model (specify which)
Both, as distinct enum members from day one (e.g. HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC_OF_DATE and HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC_J2000)

questions.question: Are V1 geocentric states geometric (instantaneous true positions) or apparent (light-time corrected, and optionally with annual aberration and nutation)? 001 §16 defines geocentric position purely as Planet_heliocentric − Earth_heliocentric, which is geometric; none of the documents mention light-time, aberration, or nutation anywhere.
questions.why_it_matters: Light-time alone is up to ~40 arcminutes for Jupiter and tens of arcminutes for the outer planets — an order of magnitude larger than the stated 1–2 arcminute target — so this single choice decides whether the model can pass its own accuracy contract. It also fixes which Horizons quantity the fixtures must use (astrometric vs apparent vs geometric vectors) and whether GEOCENTRIC_EQUATORIAL uses mean or true obliquity.
options: V1 is geometric only; document the omission explicitly as a known limitation and validate against Horizons geometric vectors
V1 applies light-time correction for geocentric frames, but not aberration or nutation; validate against Horizons astrometric positions
V1 applies light-time + annual aberration + nutation for geocentric frames; validate against Horizons apparent positions
Geometric by default, with apparent corrections exposed as an explicit opt-in transform/frame

questions.question: Which time scale is actually fed to the Schlyter equations, and does V1 implement UTC→TT conversion? 002 §3 requires distinguishing UTC, TT/TDB and simulation time and says the API must not bake in the day-number assumption, but never says whether the day number d is derived from UTC, UT1, or TT — nor whether a leap-second table or delta-T model is in scope.
questions.why_it_matters: It determines whether H003 must ship a leap-second/delta-T table (a real data dependency with a maintenance story) or can treat JD(UTC) as the model input. It is also the difference between roughly 40 arcseconds of lunar position error and none, and it fixes what the response field "scale": "UTC" actually asserts about the computation.
options: V1 feeds JD(UTC) directly to the model, documents the UT1/TT approximation as a known limitation, and the TimeScale enum exists but only UTC is implemented
V1 implements a delta-T polynomial (name the source, e.g. Espenak–Meeus) and feeds TT to the models while reporting UTC at the boundary
V1 ships a leap-second table for TAI/TT and a UT1-UTC of zero assumption

questions.question: What are the actual per-body warning and failure tolerances? 006 §11 gives the shape (SCHLYTER_PLANETS_V1: angular: warning: ..., failure: ...) with literal ellipses and forbids a single universal tolerance, and 002 §22 only gives an aggregate '1–2 arcminutes' engineering target.
questions.why_it_matters: Validation tasks H006/H008/H010/H012/H014 cannot be written without pass/fail numbers, and 005 §9 forbids an agent from adjusting a tolerance to make a build pass — so the numbers must come from you, not from whatever the implementation happens to produce. Distance tolerances (absolute and relative) are similarly undefined.
options: You supply a table now (angular warning/failure per body, plus distance tolerances)

Start with a uniform provisional 2'/5' warning/failure for planets and 5'/15' for the Moon, then ratchet each body down to its measured worst case once the first validation report exists (ratcheting recorded as an ADR)
Derive tolerances empirically in the first validation run and freeze them as regression baselines, accepting whatever the model achieves

questions.question: How do the validation fixtures in tests/fixtures/ephemeris/ actually get produced — is there network access to JPL Horizons during development, is there a committed generation script an agent may run, or will you supply the reference data by hand? 006 §7 mandates the Horizons → fixture → commit → CI flow and forbids querying Horizons in CI, but never says who runs the query or when.
questions.why_it_matters: This is an undeclared external dependency on the critical path of every validation task. If harness agents have no network access, they cannot generate reference data and would be tempted to fabricate 'expected' values from their own implementation — which would make the entire validation subsystem circular and worthless.
options: Agents may call the Horizons API from a committed script (scripts/generate-fixtures) during fixture tasks; the script records source, retrieval date, and full query configuration
You will generate and commit fixtures manually before each validation task; agents may only consume them
A one-time bulk fixture set is generated up front for all bodies/dates in the plan, and agents never regenerate

questions.question: Is Pluto in V1? 001 §3.1 makes it conditional ('if its ephemeris model is sufficiently defined'), 002 §18 lists PLUTO as a required registry identifier, but the 004 scene graph, the 007 Milestone 2 body list, and harness tasks H007–H012 all omit it.
questions.why_it_matters: Pluto in Schlyter's tutorial is not a Keplerian element set but a special-case trigonometric series valid only 1800–2100 with ~1 arcminute accuracy — a materially different code path, model ID, date range, and validation fixture set. It also changes whether GET /api/v1/bodies advertises it and whether the renderer needs a tenth body plus a highly inclined orbit path.
options: PLUTO exists in the registry enum but is not implemented in V1; requesting it returns UnsupportedBodyError
Implement Pluto in V1 as its own model ID (e.g. SCHLYTER_PLUTO_V1) with its own 1800–2100 range and tolerance, rendered like the planets
Implement Pluto's model but exclude it from the default renderer scene and default bodies list

questions.question: Which (body, frame) combinations must V1 support, and what happens for the degenerate or unnatural ones — the Sun in HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC (the origin), the Earth in GEOCENTRIC_* (the origin), and the Moon in HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC (which requires adding Earth's heliocentric position to a geocentric lunar state)? 002 §19 mentions 'supported frames' in body metadata but no matrix is given.
questions.why_it_matters: It determines whether the engine returns a zero vector, throws UnsupportedReferenceFrameError, or performs a composition for these cases — and whether the API must reject a body/frame pair with 400/422. The example response in 003 §8 shows EARTH at (0,0,0) in HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC, which is very likely a placeholder error and should be confirmed.
options: All 11 bodies are valid in all three V1 frames; degenerate cases return an exact zero vector rather than an error, and the Moon is composed via Earth heliocentric + geocentric Moon
Degenerate combinations (Sun/heliocentric, Earth/geocentric) return UnsupportedReferenceFrameError
You supply an explicit body×frame support matrix that the registry encodes and the API validates against

questions.question: What does the ephemeris response actually contain per body beyond position and distance — spherical coordinates (ecliptic lon/lat, RA/Dec), velocity, per-body accuracy metadata, name/type? The conceptual response in 003 §8 shows only position and distance, while 002 §17 makes sphericalCoordinates and velocity optional and 001 §2.3 lists RA/Dec/ecliptic lon/lat as things the engine should expose.
questions.why_it_matters: The body-info panel (007 Milestone 7) and any future astrology consumer need spherical coordinates; if they are not in the response, the client must either recompute them or make extra calls. Velocity is a real scope question because the Schlyter model does not yield velocities directly — it would need numerical differentiation, which is unspecified work.
options: Position + distance + spherical coordinates appropriate to the requested frame; velocity omitted in V1 (the CelestialState.velocity field stays undefined)
Add velocity via documented numerical differentiation (state a step size and accuracy claim)
Position + distance only; spherical conversion is a client-side concern using shared conversion utilities

questions.question: For GET /api/v1/ephemeris: what is the default when `bodies` is omitted, what is the maximum list length ('excessively large' with only ~11 valid IDs), is `bodies=` (empty) a 400 or a 200 with an empty array, are duplicates a 400 or silently de-duplicated, and are IDs case-sensitive (003 §6 shows `SUN,EARTH,MARS` while 001 §23 shows `sun,earth,mars`)? What ordering does the response use — request order or a canonical order?
questions.why_it_matters: 003 §21 requires explicit tests for 'empty body list' and 'multiple bodies' and 006 §17 requires 'deterministic ordering', so each of these needs a defined answer before the schema layer can be written; they are exactly the cases a test would otherwise assert against whatever the implementation happened to do.
options: Omitted = all supported bodies; empty string = 400; duplicates = 400; IDs are case-insensitive on input and always uppercase in responses; results returned in canonical registry order regardless of request order
Omitted = all supported bodies; empty = 200 with empty array; duplicates de-duplicated silently; response preserves request order
`bodies` is required rather than optional

questions.question: What is the complete error `code` enum and its mapping to HTTP status? 003 §13 shows one example (INVALID_REFERENCE_FRAME) and §14 leaves 422 conditional ('if adopted by the API conventions'), while 002 §21 names six domain errors. Specifically: does an out-of-range date return 400 or 422, and does a Kepler convergence failure return 500 or 422?
questions.why_it_matters: 003 §21 requires tests for 'unsupported date range' and 'numerical error translation', which cannot be written without the mapping. A stable code enum is also part of the client contract and the 'OpenAPI can be generated later without redesigning the contract' acceptance criterion.
options: 400 for anything malformed or unparseable; 422 for well-formed but semantically unsupported (out-of-range date, unsupported body/frame combination); 500 for convergence failures, logged with the code NUMERICAL_CONVERGENCE_FAILURE
Skip 422 entirely in V1 — all client-side problems are 400; convergence failure is 500
You supply the full code→status table

questions.question: For V1 orbital paths (H020), what is the sampled time window and sample count, and where are the samples computed? 004 §12–13 permits 'fixed sampling' without a number; 003 §12 explicitly defers the batch endpoint that fixed sampling over HTTP would require. Neptune's 165-year period and Pluto's 248-year period also raise whether a path covers one full orbital period or a window around the current instant.
questions.why_it_matters: Without a decision this is either N bodies × M samples of HTTP round-trips per redraw, or an undeclared requirement for the deferred batch endpoint, or an admission that orbit paths are computed client-side — which loops back to the runtime data path question. The sample count also directly drives the frame-rate target in 004 §29.
options: One full orbital period per body, fixed 360 samples, computed client-side and regenerated only when the date changes by a meaningful fraction of a period
A window of ±X around the current instant (specify X) rather than a full period
Full period, computed server-side via the batch endpoint — which is therefore pulled into V1 scope

questions.question: What exactly does 'visualization mode' do numerically, and what would make it acceptable? 004 §6/§23 and 001 §30 say radii may be 'exaggerated' and the distance scale 'may use a separate display mapping' but define no function, no exaggeration factor, and no constraints — e.g. must a body's mesh never overlap its neighbours' orbits, and must the Moon remain visibly outside Earth's mesh at its true 0.0026 AU separation?
questions.why_it_matters: This is currently unfalsifiable: no test can tell whether H023 was implemented correctly. The Earth–Moon case is the sharpest — at true scale with an exaggerated Earth radius, the Moon renders inside the Earth mesh, so some rule is needed regardless. It also determines whether the Moon's distance gets its own separate exaggeration.
options: Visualization mode multiplies body radii by a single configurable constant (with the Sun capped separately) and leaves distances at true linear scale, with an invariant test that no mesh radius exceeds a fixed fraction of the body's distance to its parent
Visualization mode applies log-compressed distances as well as exaggerated radii (you specify the mapping)
Per-body radius multipliers tuned by hand and stored as presentation metadata, with the Earth–Moon distance separately exaggerated so the Moon stays visible

questions.question: What is the concrete rule for 'the client can request state updates at appropriate simulation intervals' / 'recompute state whenever the simulation clock advances sufficiently' (001 §25), and is the visual interpolation between recomputes linear on position? 004 §22 separates simulation tick, astronomical update, and render frame but gives no rate for the middle one.
questions.why_it_matters: 'Sufficiently' is unfalsifiable and the choice is visible: too coarse and Mercury visibly stutters or lags at high playback rates; too fine and it is one recompute per frame, which 004 §22 exists to prevent. Interpolating positions linearly is also a (small) departure from the astronomy state, which ADR-016/004 §30 would want documented.
options: Recompute on a fixed cadence (e.g. 10 Hz) regardless of playback rate; linear interpolation of scene positions in between, documented in the renderer docs
Recompute when the simulation instant has advanced past a per-body angular threshold (e.g. the fastest visible body would move more than ~0.1° on screen); no interpolation
Recompute every frame in V1 and only add throttling if profiling shows a problem (per 001 §2.6)

questions.question: What is the unit convention for SimulationClock.playbackRate, and what happens when playback reaches the edge of the supported date range? 001 §26 gives the example playbackRate = 86400 meaning one real second advances one simulation day, but explicitly hedges ('assuming the chosen rate convention. The unit convention must be explicit'). 007 Milestone 9 and 001 §45 list preset speeds up to 1 year/sec with no stated bounds.
questions.why_it_matters: Two defensible readings (simulation-seconds per real-second vs a multiplier over an implied base) give results differing by orders of magnitude, and the preset list must map onto whichever is chosen. Range-edge behaviour is entirely unspecified: pausing, clamping, wrapping, and erroring are all plausible and all visible to the user.
options: playbackRate is simulation-seconds per real-second (86400 = 1 day/sec), sign carries direction; on reaching a range boundary the clock clamps and auto-pauses
Same unit convention, but the clock stops with a user-visible message rather than silently pausing
playbackRate is simulation-days per real-second (1 = 1 day/sec)

questions.question: Where do the non-computed body data come from — physical radii and masses (which source and epoch?), and textures/colors (which asset set and license)? 002 §19 lists 'physical radius', 'mass if needed', and 'color/texture identifier' as metadata, and 004 §11 requires 'visual assets must have documented licenses', but no source is ever named for either.
questions.why_it_matters: 004's body rendering task (H018) cannot start without knowing whether it is drawing flat colored spheres or loading textures, and 001 §62 makes attribution a release requirement. Sourcing textures is also a licensing decision an agent must not make on its own.
options: V1 uses flat/solid colors with no external texture assets; radii and masses from the NASA/JPL planetary fact sheets, cited in docs/astronomy
Use a specific public-domain texture set (you name it, e.g. NASA/JPL imagery or Solar System Scope's CC-BY maps) with licenses recorded in a THIRD_PARTY_ASSETS file
Textures deferred to Milestone 8 (visual polish); colors only until then

questions.question: What are the default SCALE_FACTOR (scene units per AU), the Sun's and planets' radius mapping in *scientific* mode, and the camera near/far planes? 004 §6 requires one canonical convention and says 'the factor must be configurable' but gives no default, and 004 §30 requires 'physically meaningful radius mapping' in scientific mode.
questions.why_it_matters: At true linear scale Earth is roughly 1/23,000 of an AU across, so scientific mode with a naive mapping renders every planet as a sub-pixel dot and the default view looks broken. Near/far plane ratios at AU scale also drive the depth-precision artifacts flagged in 004 §26, and a bad default would trigger premature optimization work.
options: 1 AU = 100 scene units; scientific mode uses true radii (accepting sub-pixel planets at solar-system-wide zoom) with a documented minimum-pixel-size floor for visibility
1 AU = 1 scene unit with a logarithmic depth buffer
You specify the default factor and the scientific-mode radius rule

questions.question: Which ADR numbering is canonical — 001 §42 or Document 008? They disagree: 001 §42 assigns ADR-004 to 'self-contained astronomy engine' and ADR-005 to 'Horizons for validation', while 008 assigns ADR-004 to Express, ADR-005 to No Database, ADR-006 to self-contained astronomy, and ADR-007 to Horizons. 001 §42's list also stops at ADR-008 (astrology separation), which 008 numbers ADR-014.

options: Document 008 is canonical; 001 §42 is superseded and should be edited to reference 008 rather than list numbers
001 §42 is canonical and 008 should be renumbered
Leave both and treat 001 §42 as an informal list of ADR *topics* with no binding numbers

questions.question: Will V1 be publicly deployed, and if so at what origin(s)? 003 §18 makes rate limiting conditional ('if publicly exposed') and requires a CORS allowlist without naming any origins; 007 Milestone 10 lists 'deployment' as a deliverable with no target.

If the app is a static GitHub Pages demo with a browser-side astronomy package, the API may never be publicly hosted, which changes 003 §18 substantially.
options: Local/self-hosted only for V1; CORS allowlist is localhost plus a configurable env var, rate limiting implemented but disabled by default
Publicly deployed (name the host/domain); rate limiting on by default with a stated limit
Frontend deployed publicly as a static site with browser-side computation; the API is never publicly hosted

payload.assessment: The document set is unusually strong on structure, boundaries, and policy — package separation, unit/frame discipline, model versioning, and agent constraints are all well specified — but it is thin on the concrete numbers and physical conventions an implementer needs. The weakest areas are (a) the scientific contract itself: the equinox/epoch of the named reference frames, whether states are geometric or apparent, which time scale feeds the models, the actual supported date range, and the numeric validation tolerances are all referenced but never stated; (b) the runtime data path, where ADR-006's "self-contained runtime astronomy" contradicts the HTTP-based architecture in 001 §5/§25 and 003; and (c) the visualization/simulation layer, where scale mapping, orbit sampling, recompute cadence, and playback-rate units are described only as "configurable" or "to be decided". Everything below is a gap where a wrong guess produces silent scientific error or meaningful rework, not a style preference.

answers.answer: Document 008 is canonical; 001 §42 is superseded and should be edited to reference 008 rather than list numbers

answers.question: Will V1 be publicly deployed, and if so at what origin(s)? 003 §18 makes rate limiting conditional ('if publicly exposed') and requires a CORS allowlist without naming any origins; 007 Milestone 10 lists 'deployment' as a deliverable with no target.
answers.answer: Local/self-hosted only for V1; CORS allowlist is localhost plus a configurable env var, rate limiting implemented but disabled by default

questions.question: How do the 360 orbit samples per body physically get computed, given that all celestial state must come from the Express API? The answered question `runtime_data_path` says the frontend calls the Express API and the API uses the astronomy package, but the answer to `orbit_path_generation` says orbit paths are 'computed client-side' — which would require the astronomy package to run in the browser. With 11 bodies x 360 samples that is ~3,960 states per regeneration, and 003 §12 explicitly defers `POST /api/v1/ephemeris/batch`. Which is it?
questions.why_it_matters: This decides whether V1 must implement the batch endpoint now, whether packages/astronomy must be browser-bundlable (affecting build config, package exports, and bundle size), and whether ADR-006's offline-capability rationale applies to orbits. Guessing wrong invalidates the scope of H016 (API) and H020 (orbital paths).
questions.source: Q&A `runtime_data_path` and `orbit_path_generation`; 003 §12 Future Batch Endpoint; ADR-006
options: Implement POST /api/v1/ephemeris/batch in V1 (accepting an explicit instant list) and generate orbits server-side through it
Bundle the astronomy package into the browser and compute orbit samples client-side, keeping the HTTP API for single-instant state only
Add a dedicated server-side orbit endpoint, e.g. GET /api/v1/orbit?body=MARS&samples=360, returning a ready-made sampled path

questions.question: Does the 10 Hz recompute cadence mean up to 10 HTTP requests per second to /api/v1/ephemeris during playback, or does the client prefetch a window of instants and interpolate locally? 003 §16 says 'No cache required initially. Do not cache before profiling', and 001 §25 says 'do not request a new HTTP calculation for every animation frame' without naming an acceptable rate.
questions.why_it_matters: Determines whether V1 needs a batch/window prefetch mechanism, client-side request throttling, or server caching, and whether the answered 10 Hz figure is a computation cadence or a network cadence. It also drives the rate-limit configuration in 003 §18.
options: 10 Hz HTTP polling is acceptable for local/self-hosted V1; revisit after profiling
Client prefetches a window (e.g. the next N simulation days) in one batch request and interpolates locally between prefetches
Astronomy runs in the browser for animation; the HTTP API is used only for initial load and explicit date jumps

questions.question: Which package owns the Three.js scene, and is React Three Fiber allowed? 001 §6 shows both `apps/web/src/scene/` and `packages/renderer/src/scene/`, and 004 §8 specifies an imperative `PlanetRenderer { create() update(state) setSelected() dispose() }` while 004 §21 warns 'Avoid React state updates every animation frame'. Nothing states whether R3F/drei may be used or whether the renderer must be framework-agnostic vanilla Three.js mounted from a single React host component.
questions.why_it_matters: This determines the structure of Milestones 6-8 and harness tasks H017-H023, whether packages/renderer may depend on React (never explicitly forbidden for the renderer), and whether the PlanetRenderer lifecycle interface in 004 §8 is normative or illustrative.
options: packages/renderer is vanilla Three.js with zero React dependency; apps/web/src/scene holds only the thin React host component that mounts it
Use React Three Fiber inside apps/web and keep packages/renderer for pure adapter/scaling/coordinate logic only (no meshes)
packages/renderer may depend on React and export R3F components; drop apps/web/src/scene from the structure

questions.question: Where does model attribution live in the ephemeris response now that multiple models are in play? 003 §8 shows a single top-level `"model": "SCHLYTER_PLANETS_V1"`, but the answered questions establish a separate `SCHLYTER_PLUTO_V1`, and ADR-013 / 002 §15 establish a separate lunar model. A response containing MOON, PLUTO and MARS cannot honestly carry one top-level model ID.
questions.why_it_matters: 002 §23 makes model version essential for reproducible regression tests and 003 §22 requires 'every response has explicit frame and model'. The shape chosen here is baked into the shared TypeScript contracts, the fixture format (006 §6), and any future OpenAPI document.
options: Move `modelId` onto each body entry and drop the top-level field
Keep a top-level `models` map listing every model used in the response, plus per-body `modelId`
Keep the top-level field as the primary planetary model and add per-body `modelId` only where it differs

questions.question: What exactly does `GET /api/v1/bodies` return, and is it the source for the UI's body-info panel? 003 §5 says only 'Returns body metadata and supported calculation models.' Does each entry include display name, type (star/planet/dwarf planet/moon), parent body, physical radius with unit, mass, supported frames, model ID, accuracy metadata, and the supported date range? And does the body-info panel (001 §3.6, Milestone 7) render from this endpoint plus live ephemeris values, or from a hardcoded frontend table?
questions.why_it_matters: This is a whole endpoint with no schema, and it is the only candidate source for the UI's static body data and for the date-range bounds the timeline control must clamp against. Guessing wrong means duplicated metadata in the frontend (violating 002 §19's 'metadata separately from algorithms') or a second round of API changes during Milestone 7.
options: Full metadata per body (id, displayName, type, parentBody, radius {value,unit}, mass {value,unit}, supportedFrames, modelId, accuracy, supportedDateRange) and the info panel renders from it
Minimal metadata (id, displayName, type, supportedFrames, modelId); physical constants and textures live in the renderer's presentation registry
Full metadata as above plus a separate GET /api/v1/capabilities carrying frames, models, and the global supported date range

questions.question: Which `instant` string forms does the API accept, exactly? 003 §7 says 'ISO-8601 timestamps are preferred' — implying something else is also accepted — and shows only a Z form and a -04:00 offset as good. Is a bare date ('2026-08-14') accepted, and at what time of day? Is a raw Julian Date accepted? Are fractional seconds accepted? Is the literal 'now' accepted, given 003 §17 forbids responses depending on current server time?
questions.why_it_matters: This is the primary input of the whole API and drives the runtime validation schema plus the 'invalid timestamp' and 'missing timestamp' tests required by 003 §21. 'Preferred' rather than 'required' leaves the accepted set genuinely undefined.
options: ISO-8601 with a mandatory Z or +/-HH:MM offset only; everything else is 400 (no bare dates, no 'now', no raw JD)
As above, plus a bare date interpreted as 00:00:00Z
As above, plus a separate optional `julianDate` parameter for raw JD input

questions.question: In what time zone does the web UI accept and display dates? 003 §7 requires an explicit offset at the HTTP boundary and 001 §24 says the API must 'reject ambiguous dates', but nothing says whether the date picker and on-screen clock work in UTC, in the browser's local zone (converted before the request), or in a user-selectable zone. 002 §2: 'A civil date/time is not an instant until its time-zone interpretation is known.'
questions.why_it_matters: It changes the date-input component, the status-bar time display, the E2E expectations in 006 §19 ('date changes'), and whether every reported validation date and screenshot is UTC or local. It is the most likely source of silent off-by-hours bugs.
options: UTC everywhere in the UI, labelled explicitly; no local-time affordance in V1
Browser local zone for input and display, converted to an explicit offset before every request, with the UTC equivalent always shown alongside
User-selectable display zone defaulting to browser local, stored in UI state only

questions.question: What is the application's state on first load? 006 §19 requires an E2E test that 'default solar system appears', but nothing defines the defaults: which reference frame, which instant (browser 'now' or a fixed demo date), which rendering mode (scientific or visualization), whether playback starts paused, which bodies are visible, and whether orbit paths and labels start enabled.
questions.why_it_matters: Every E2E scenario in 006 §19 asserts against this state, and the choice between 'now' and a fixed date determines whether the default view is reproducible in tests and screenshots.
options: Heliocentric, visualization mode, current browser time, paused, all bodies visible, orbits on, labels on
Same but with a fixed default instant (e.g. 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) so first render is deterministic and testable, plus a 'Now' button
Heliocentric, scientific mode, current time, paused, orbits off, labels off (minimal first paint, user opts in)

questions.question: What do orbit paths show in geocentric view? 004 §24 defines geocentric rendering as `scenePosition = bodyPosition - earthPosition`, and the answer to `orbit_path_generation` fixes 'one full orbital period per body, fixed 360 samples'. Sampled geocentrically that produces apparent retrograde loops, and a full 165-year Neptune path in geocentric coordinates is a very different object from its heliocentric ellipse. Are orbit paths drawn at all in geocentric mode, and if so are they sampled in the geocentric frame?
questions.why_it_matters: Determines whether the client regenerates all paths on every frame switch, whether 360 samples is adequate for a geocentric outer-planet path, or whether the orbit layer is simply hidden geocentrically. It also affects the E2E 'orbital paths toggle' scenario.
options: Yes — sample in the requested frame, so geocentric paths show true apparent/retrograde loops, regenerated on frame switch
No — hide the orbit layer in geocentric mode for V1 and document the limitation
Geocentric paths show only a short window around the current instant (e.g. +/-1 year) instead of a full period

questions.question: Which concrete tools does Milestone 0 / task H001 install? 007 §2 lists 'package manager/workspaces, lint, formatting, unit test runner, CI' and 001 §67 requires 'tests execute, lint executes, typecheck executes, CI executes', but no tool is ever named. options: pnpm workspaces + TS project references + Vitest + Vite + Playwright + Zod + GitHub Actions
npm workspaces + Vitest + Vite + Playwright + Zod + GitHub Actions (fewest moving parts)
pnpm + Turborepo for task orchestration and caching, otherwise as above
Any of the above — pick sensible defaults and record them in an ADR

questions.question: Do rendered bodies rotate on their axes in V1, and with what tilt? 001 §2.3 lists 'body orientation where supported' among engine outputs, but 002 has no rotation model and no rotation period or pole orientation in the §19 metadata list, and 004 never mentions spin or axial tilt (rings are already deferred by 004 §11).

options: Not in V1 — unrotated spheres, documented as a known visual limitation
Cosmetic only — apply documented axial tilt and sidereal rotation period from a cited source as renderer presentation metadata, explicitly not an astronomy-engine output
Full scope — add body orientation (pole RA/Dec + rotation) to the astronomy domain with validation

questions.question: What clients must V1 support? 004 §29 and 001 §36 target '60 FPS on modern desktop' only, while 004 §17 asks for a 'pan gesture', implying touch. Is mobile/tablet in V1 scope, and which browsers and Node version are supported (i.e. what does CI test against and what does the README onboarding claim)?

options: Desktop Chrome/Firefox/Safari (current) only, mouse+keyboard, no responsive work in V1; Node 20 LTS
Desktop as above plus basic pointer/touch support so tablets work, but no dedicated mobile layout
Full responsive and touch support including phones, with a reduced-quality rendering path

payload.assessment: The architecture set is unusually thorough on domain vocabulary, units, frames, and validation policy, and the first Q&A round closed most of the scientific-model gaps (date range, equinox, geometric-only states, time scale, body/frame matrix, tolerances). The weakest remaining area is the client/server data path: the answers to `runtime_data_path` (all state comes from the Express API), `orbit_path_generation` (360 client-side samples per body per orbit) and `recompute_cadence` (10 Hz recompute) cannot all be satisfied with only the single-instant GET endpoint that 003 defines, and 003 §12 explicitly defers the batch endpoint that would make them possible. questions.question: How are orbit paths generated for bodies whose orbital period exceeds the supported date range? The accepted answers fix the range at 1900-01-01 to 2100-01-01 UTC with a hard UnsupportedDateRangeError outside it, and fix orbit paths at 'one full orbital period per body, fixed 360 samples'. Those cannot both hold: Pluto's period is ~248 years and Neptune's ~165 years, so a full-period sample set centred on any date in the 2020s requires instants outside the supported range (and Uranus at ~84 years fails for dates near either end of the range). Should the sampler clamp to the supported range and draw a partial arc, should the range be widened for orbit sampling only, or should long-period bodies use a different path source (e.g. a static ellipse drawn from their osculating orbital elements rather than sampled states)?
questions.why_it_matters: Determines whether the orbit layer calls the astronomy engine with out-of-range instants (which the engine is specified to reject), and whether Neptune/Pluto show a closed ellipse or an open arc. It changes both the sampler's contract and the error behaviour of the batch endpoint.
options: Clamp sampling to the supported range and draw a partial (open) arc for any body whose period does not fit
Allow orbit sampling to exceed the supported range internally (path generation is exempt from UnsupportedDateRangeError)
Draw long-period orbits from osculating orbital elements as a geometric ellipse instead of sampled states
Cap every path at a fixed window (e.g. min(period, 30 years)) regardless of body

questions.question: Where does astronomical computation actually execute at runtime, and does packages/astronomy ship a browser build? Three accepted answers point in different directions: runtime_data_path says 'Express API are called from the frontend/client. The API's use the Astronomy Package'; recompute_transport_cadence says 'Astronomy runs in the browser for animation; the HTTP API is used only for initial load and explicit date jumps'; orbit_sample_transport says orbits are 'generated server-side' through POST /api/v1/ephemeris/batch. Please state the final split — which of {initial load, date jump, 10 Hz playback recompute, orbit path generation, body metadata} is served over HTTP and which is computed in-browser — and confirm whether the astronomy package is therefore a bundled browser dependency of apps/web.
questions.why_it_matters: This decides whether apps/web depends on packages/astronomy directly (changing the dependency graph in 001 §5/§20 and the bundle/build setup), whether the Express API is on the critical path at all after first load, and whether the HTTP layer or the in-browser engine is the authority when both could answer the same query.
questions.source: Answered questions runtime_data_path, recompute_transport_cadence, orbit_sample_transport; 001 §5, §25; ADR-006
options: Browser computes everything for interaction (playback, orbits); the API exists for /bodies, initial load, and as a documented server-side surface
Server computes everything (single ephemeris/batch path); the browser only interpolates between server responses
Hybrid as literally answered: server for initial load, date jumps, and orbit batches; browser only for the 10 Hz playback recompute

questions.question: What is the request and response contract for POST /api/v1/ephemeris/batch, now that it is in V1? 003 §12 only says it 'should accept an explicit list of instants rather than an ambiguous "generate everything" request'. Specifically: is it one flat instants list applied to all requested bodies (which forces one request per body for orbits, since each body needs its own period-length list), or per-body instant lists in a single request? What is the maximum number of instants and of (body x instant) pairs, and what status is returned when exceeded (400 vs 413 vs 429)? Is the response an array of the same per-instant objects defined in 003 §8, and is ordering guaranteed to match the request order of instants?
questions.why_it_matters: Orbit generation for 11 bodies x 360 samples is ~3,960 states; the request shape determines whether that is 1 request or 11, interacts directly with the 'request size limits' required by 003 §18, and fixes the client-side orbit sampler's implementation.
options: Per-body instant lists in one request: { frame, bodies: [{ id, instants: [...] }] }, response mirrors that structure
Flat list: { frame, bodies: [...], instants: [...] } evaluated as a cross-product; orbits issue one request per body
Flat list, but capped at N total (body x instant) pairs with 400 + BATCH_TOO_LARGE beyond it

questions.question: How are of-date positions validated against JPL Horizons, which does not emit mean-ecliptic-of-date vectors? The accepted answers set V1 frames to 'mean equinox and ecliptic of date' and defer precession ('add explicit J2000-suffixed frame identifiers later when a precession model is implemented'), while 006 §7 mandates Horizons-derived fixtures. Horizons vector output is referenced to J2000 (or B1950), so comparing our of-date output directly against it introduces a precession offset of roughly 0.3-0.4 degrees per century — one to two orders of magnitude larger than the 1-2 arcminute target, which would make every fixture fail for reasons unrelated to the model. Do we implement Schlyter's precession purely as validation-side infrastructure, generate fixtures from a Horizons product that is already of-date (e.g. observer-table RA/Dec of date), or store J2000 fixtures and rotate them at test time?
questions.why_it_matters: Without an answer the entire validation programme (H006/H008/H010/H012/H014 and Milestone 2's exit criteria) cannot produce a meaningful pass/fail, and the empirically-derived tolerances would bake in a precession error as if it were model error.
options: Implement precession now and rotate our of-date result to J2000 inside the validation harness only
Generate fixtures from Horizons output that is already referred to the equinox of date (observer tables), and validate angularly against those
Store J2000 fixtures plus a committed precession rotation applied in the test, documented as validation-only code

questions.question: Is precess(state, fromEpoch, toEpoch) implemented as a shipped public API in V1, and if so which precession model? 002 §16 requires the transformation and says 'The supported model and validity range must be documented'; Milestone 3 lists 'precession support as required by model' and H015 covers coordinate transformations. But the accepted frame answer says all V1 frames are of-date and J2000-suffixed frames come 'later', which leaves precession with no runtime consumer. Is it (a) not built in V1, (b) built as a public but unused API, or (c) built only inside the validation harness?
questions.why_it_matters: Determines whether H015 and Milestone 3 include a precession implementation and its tests, and whether the astronomy package's public surface in v0.1/v0.2 includes precess(). It also interacts with the fixture question above.
options: Yes - implement Schlyter's simple precession as a public API now, documented with its validity range, even though no V1 frame consumes it
Validation-only: implement it in the test/validation layer, keep it out of the package's public API until J2000 frames exist
Defer entirely to a later milestone; 002 §16 is a reserved design slot, not V1 work

questions.question: For the newly in-scope body orientation work ('add body orientation (pole RA/Dec + rotation) to the astronomy domain with validation'), what is the source model, which bodies, and how does orientation reach the renderer? None of the documents specify a rotation model: 002 §19's metadata list has no rotation period or pole, 002 §17's CelestialState has no orientation field, and the accepted response-payload answer fixes the ephemeris body entry at position + distance + spherical coordinates only. Concretely: is the source the IAU WGCCRE report on cartographic coordinates and rotational elements (which edition?) or Horizons-derived constants? Does it cover all 11 bodies including the Moon's synchronous rotation and libration? Is orientation a new field on CelestialState and on the API response, with its own model ID and tolerance? And is it validated numerically or only asserted against published constants?
questions.why_it_matters: This is a whole new computational subsystem with its own reference source, frame convention (pole RA/Dec is equatorial-of-J2000 in the IAU model, which conflicts with our of-date frames), state field, response field, and validation fixtures - none of which exists in any document. Without it, the harness has no task contract to build against.
options: IAU WGCCRE rotational elements (pole RA/Dec + W) for all 11 bodies, exposed as a new orientation field on CelestialState and the API response, with its own model ID (e.g. IAU_WGCCRE_ORIENTATION_V1)
Same model, but orientation stays presentation metadata in the renderer/body registry and never appears in CelestialState or the API
Narrow it: constant axial tilt + constant rotation period per body from a cited table, no time-varying pole, validated only as a round-trip/continuity test

questions.question: What is the exact astronomy-to-scene axis mapping? 004 §5 and 001 §29 both require the adapter to define 'axis mapping, handedness, unit scaling, origin, orientation' and say 'Document the exact transformation mathematically' - but no document ever states it. Our ecliptic Cartesian frame is right-handed with +z north of the ecliptic (002 §8); Three.js convention is right-handed with +y up. Is the mapping scene(x,y,z) = astro(x, z, -y) (ecliptic plane becomes the scene's horizontal XZ plane, ecliptic north becomes scene +y), or a direct identity mapping with the camera's up vector set to +z, or something else?
questions.why_it_matters: This is the single documented boundary between science and presentation and the subject of a required unit test (004 §28, 006 §18). Choosing wrong flips the apparent direction of planetary motion (prograde would render clockwise from ecliptic north) and silently mirrors the scene - a defect that looks plausible and is easy to miss.
options: scene.x = astro.x, scene.y = astro.z, scene.z = -astro.y (ecliptic plane maps to Three.js XZ ground plane, ecliptic north to +Y; preserves handedness and prograde sense viewed from +Y)
Identity mapping (scene.xyz = astro.xyz) with camera up set to (0,0,1), keeping ecliptic north as scene +Z
Some other mapping you want documented explicitly in the adapter doc

questions.question: With React Three Fiber chosen and packages/renderer restricted to 'pure adapter/scaling/coordinate logic only (no meshes)', do 004 §8's imperative PlanetRenderer interface (create/update/setSelected/dispose) and 004 §9's celestial body registry (mesh factory, texture, material, radius strategy, label, orbit renderer) still stand, and where do they now live? questions.question: What does the orbit layer draw for the Sun and the Moon in each frame? The accepted rule is 'one full orbital period per body, fixed 360 samples, sampled in the requested frame'. questions.question: In which frame, and as seen from which centre, is the '1-2 arcminute' accuracy figure measured and reported? 006 §9 defines angular error as the angle between two vectors, which is frame- and origin-dependent: the same position error yields a very different angular error measured from the Sun than from Earth (dramatically so for Venus or Mars near opposition, and for the Moon). 002 §22 states the target without naming a centre, and the accepted tolerance answer defers the numbers to the first validation run without fixing the metric. payload.assessment: The architecture set is unusually thorough on boundaries, units, frames, and process discipline, and Round 1–2 answers have closed most of the big scope holes. The weakest areas now are (a) internal consistency between the Round 2 answers themselves — where astronomy actually executes at runtime, and orbit paths whose "one full orbital period" exceeds the accepted 1900–2100 date range; (b) the validation chain, where of-date frames cannot be compared to Horizons J2000 vectors without a precession model that V1 may not have; and (c) two areas newly promoted into scope with no spec behind them — the POST batch endpoint and body axial orientation/rotation. The Three.js layer is also still missing the one thing document 004 says must be documented mathematically: the actual astronomy→scene axis mapping.

answers.question: How are orbit paths generated for bodies whose orbital period exceeds the supported date range? The accepted answers fix the range at 1900-01-01 to 2100-01-01 UTC with a hard UnsupportedDateRangeError outside it, and fix orbit paths at 'one full orbital period per body, fixed 360 samples'. Those cannot both hold: Pluto's period is ~248 years and Neptune's ~165 years, so a full-period sample set centred on any date in the 2020s requires instants outside the supported range (and Uranus at ~84 years fails for dates near either end of the range). Should the sampler clamp to the supported range and draw a partial arc, should the range be widened for orbit sampling only, or should long-period bodies use a different path source (e.g. a static ellipse drawn from their osculating orbital elements rather than sampled states)?

The weakest remaining areas are concentrated where the Round 3 answers changed the architecture: the runtime data path is now "server computes everything" but no playback fetch/prefetch contract exists to replace the discarded in-browser 10 Hz recompute, and the batch endpoint that all orbit generation now depends on still has no limits, ordering, or response shape. The validation subsystem is the other soft spot — the Horizons query configuration (center codes, product, corrections) and the fidelity of the of-date-to-J2000 rotation both directly determine whether every fixture passes or fails for reasons unrelated to the model. The remainder are smaller contract details: rotation phase epoch, spherical-coordinate units, visualization constants, and geocentric orbit sampling density.

answers.question: Now that the server computes every celestial state and "the browser only interpolates between server responses", what is the concrete fetch contract during continuous playback? Specifically: does the client prefetch a window of instants via POST /api/v1/ephemeris/batch (how many instants, how far ahead, re-fetched when?), or does it poll GET /api/v1/ephemeris at some interval? And is the earlier accepted 10 Hz recompute cadence now the interpolation-sample spacing in simulation time, or the HTTP request rate?
answers.answer: Client prefetches a rolling window via the batch endpoint (state window length in simulation time and number of instants), interpolates linearly within it, re-fetches when the window is N% consumed

answers.question: What exact JPL Horizons configuration produces the fixtures? Concretely: (a) for HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC, is the center the Sun's body center (500@10) or the solar-system barycenter (500@0)? (b) for GEOCENTRIC_*, Earth's center (500@399) or the Earth-Moon barycenter (500@3)? (c) are targets body centers or system barycenters for the giant planets (e.g. 599 vs 5)? (d) which product - VECTORS with corrections=NONE, or an observer table?
answers.answer: Sun body center (500@10) and Earth body center (500@399), planet body centers as targets, VECTORS with corrections=NONE

answers.question: Which precession formulation does the validation harness use to rotate our mean-of-date results into J2000, and how is that rotation's own error bounded? Schlyter's precession is a longitude-only correction; it does not model the ~47 arcsec/century rotation of the ecliptic plane itself, leaving a latitude/plane residual of order an arcminute per century - the same magnitude as the model error being measured. Simple longitude term, or a full ecliptic precession rotation matrix (e.g. IAU 1976/2006) inside the harness only? And which obliquity value/model converts between ecliptic and equatorial J2000 for comparison against Horizons vectors?
answers.answer: Public precess() uses Schlyter's simple longitude term; the harness uses a separate full ecliptic precession matrix (IAU 1976) plus fixed J2000 obliquity 84381.448 arcsec, with the harness residual documented

answers.question: For the accepted orbit rule "cap every path at a fixed window (e.g. min(period, 30 years))", is that window centred on the current instant (t-15y to t+15y), forward-only, or anchored otherwise - and what happens when it crosses 1900-01-01 or 2100-01-01? With a hard UnsupportedDateRangeError outside the range, a centred 30-year window fails for any date before 1915 or after 2085. Separately, what is the concrete regeneration trigger ("a meaningful fraction of a period") during continuous playback - is orbit regeneration suppressed while playing?
answers.answer: Centred on the current instant and clamped to the supported range (truncated arc near range edges)

answers.question: For POST /api/v1/ephemeris/batch with the accepted shape { frame, bodies, instants } as a cross-product: what is the maximum number of instants, the maximum number of (body x instant) pairs, and which status is returned when exceeded (400, 413, or 429)? Is the response an array of the per-instant objects from 003 section 8, or a flatter/columnar form? Is result ordering guaranteed to match the request order of instants (given bodies are always in canonical registry order)?
answers.answer: Max 500 instants; exceeding returns 413; response is columnar (shared frame/model header plus parallel arrays per body) to keep payloads small

answers.question: For the narrowed body-orientation scope (constant axial tilt plus constant rotation period from a cited table): (a) which table/edition is the citation - IAU WGCCRE report (which year?) or Horizons-derived constants? (b) is an absolute rotation phase required, i.e. a defined prime-meridian angle W0 at a reference epoch so Earth's sub-solar point is physically correct, or is phase arbitrary provided it is continuous and reproducible? (c) does orientation cross the HTTP boundary per instant, or does the renderer derive spin locally from /api/v1/bodies metadata plus the instant?
answers.answer: Cite IAU WGCCRE 2015 constants, include W0 so absolute phase is physically correct, derive spin client-side from /bodies metadata (response payload unchanged)

answers.question: Does the fixed 360-sample count still apply when orbits are sampled in a geocentric frame? Over the accepted min(period, 30 years) window, Neptune geocentric gets roughly one sample per 30 days, which aliases the ~1-year retrograde loop structure into a jagged polyline that misrepresents the apparent path. Should geocentric paths use a shorter window, a higher sample count, or is aliasing acceptable for V1?
answers.answer: Keep 360 samples but shorten the geocentric window (e.g. min(period, 5 years)) so retrograde structure is resolved

answers.question: Is the headline accuracy figure a geometric or an apparent geocentric direction error? Round 1 fixed V1 as geometric only (no light-time, aberration, or nutation) validated against Horizons geometric vectors, but Round 3 names the headline metric "geocentric apparent-direction angular error". Annual aberration alone reaches ~20 arcseconds, a meaningful fraction of a 1-2 arcminute budget, so the two are not interchangeable. Which is measured, and how is the README wording constrained so it does not imply sky-position accuracy the engine does not deliver?
answers.answer: Geometric geocentric direction error is the measured metric; the README says geometric explicitly and states light-time and aberration are not applied

answers.question: What are the exact field names and units of the per-body spherical coordinates in the ephemeris response for each frame? For the ecliptic frames, longitude/latitude in degrees or radians? For GEOCENTRIC_EQUATORIAL, is right ascension in hours (002 section 6 provides hoursToRadians/radiansToHours) or degrees, and are the fields named rightAscension/declination with an explicit unit tag like every other quantity?
answers.answer: Degrees for all spherical angles including RA, each with an explicit unit field, plus radius/distance in AU

answers.question: What are the concrete numbers for visualization mode: the radius exaggeration multiplier, the separate Sun cap, and the "fixed fraction of the body's distance to its parent" used by the invariant test? At 1 AU = 100 scene units, Earth's true radius is ~0.0043 units and the Moon sits ~0.26 units away, so a multiplier above roughly 30-60 swallows the Moon inside Earth's mesh - while a multiplier that low leaves Mercury nearly invisible at system-wide zoom.

answers.question: Is the Node CLI described in 001 section 66 (astronomy calculate --body mars --date ... --frame ...) a V1 deliverable, and if so which package owns it and is it covered by the CI gates? answers.question: Now that modelId is per-body, what is the complete list of model identifiers for V1 and which bodies map to each? SCHLYTER_PLANETS_V1 and SCHLYTER_PLUTO_V1 are established; what are the IDs for the Moon (ADR-013 mandates a separate lunar model) and for the Sun/Earth pair, given 002 section 13 requires distinguishing the apparent solar position from Earth's heliocentric position? Do SUN and EARTH share one ID or carry different ones?

questions.question: The accepted visualization constants are mutually inconsistent for the Earth-Moon system. At 1 AU = 100 scene units with a 50x radius multiplier and true linear distances: Earth's mesh radius is 6371 km / 149.6e6 km * 100 * 50 = 0.213 scene units, while the Moon orbits at 384,400 km = 0.257 scene units with a mesh radius of 0.058 units. The Moon's near edge therefore sits at 0.199 units - inside Earth's mesh - and the Moon also fails the accepted invariant (0.058 / 0.257 = 22.6% > 20% of distance to parent). How should this be resolved?
questions.why_it_matters: H018/H023 cannot implement visualization mode as specified: either the multiplier, the invariant, or the linear-distance rule for satellites must change, and the choice determines whether the renderer needs a per-system scale override mechanism at all.
questions.source: Accepted answers visualization_scale_constants (50x, Sun capped 5x, mesh radius <= 20% of distance to parent) and visualization_scale_rules (distances stay true linear); 004 sections 6-7
options: Give the Earth-Moon system its own visualization override: exaggerate the Moon's orbital distance (e.g. 8x) in visualization mode only, keeping the 50x radius multiplier and the 20% invariant intact
Cap Earth's multiplier separately (as the Sun already is) so its mesh stays well inside the lunar orbit, everything else unchanged
Lower the global multiplier to a value that satisfies the invariant for every body including the Moon (roughly <= 20x) and accept that Mercury is small at system-wide zoom
Exempt satellites from the invariant and accept that the Moon clips into Earth in visualization mode

questions.question: With the server computing all states and the browser only interpolating, what caps the spacing between computed instants in *simulation* time, and what are the concrete prefetch numbers? The accepted cadence answer fixed 10 Hz 'regardless of playback rate'; at the 1 year/sec preset that is ~36.5 simulation days between samples, so Mercury (88-day period) gets ~2.4 samples per orbit and linear interpolation collapses its orbit into a wobbling triangle. Separately, the accepted fetch answer left its own parameters as placeholders: what is the window length in simulation time, how many instants per window, and at what consumption percentage does the client re-fetch?
questions.why_it_matters: H021/H022 cannot be built without these numbers, and without a simulation-time cap on sample spacing, fast playback renders visibly wrong positions - a scientific-integrity problem, not just a visual one.
questions.source: Accepted answers recompute_cadence (10 Hz), compute_location_contradiction (server computes everything), playback_fetch_contract (window length and instant count left as placeholders); 004 section 22; 001 section 25
options: Cap spacing in simulation time so the fastest visible body gets >= 60 samples per orbit (~1.5 days), letting the HTTP request rate fall out of playbackRate, with a hard playbackRate cap where that would exceed the 500-instant batch limit
Keep a fixed 10 Hz HTTP cadence but make each request a batch whose instants subdivide the interval finely enough for the fastest body, interpolating between sub-samples
Fixed prefetch window of e.g. 30 real seconds of playback / 300 instants, re-fetched at 60% consumption, spacing = playbackRate * 0.1 s, with no orbit-relative cap
Keep 10 Hz spacing and use Catmull-Rom instead of linear interpolation

questions.question: When is the orbit layer regenerated during continuous playback? The accepted rules make each path a min(period, 30y) window (5y geocentric) *centred on the current instant* with 360 samples, generated server-side via one batch request per body - so during playback the window goes stale continuously and a full refresh is 11 requests x 360 instants. Round 3 said 'regenerated only when the date changes by a meaningful fraction of a period' without fixing the fraction, and Round 4's anchoring answer did not say whether regeneration is suppressed while playing.
questions.why_it_matters: This sets the API load profile during playback and whether orbit paths visibly lag or jump; H020 needs a concrete trigger, and the 'centred window' rule is unimplementable at 1 year/sec without one.
questions.source: Accepted answers orbit_path_generation, orbit_window_anchoring, geocentric_orbit_sampling_density, orbit_sample_transport; 004 sections 12-13
options: Suppress regeneration while playing: regenerate on pause, on explicit date jump, and on frame switch only, letting the drawn window drift off-centre during playback
Regenerate when the current instant moves more than 10% of the window length from the window centre, throttled to at most one full refresh per N seconds
Anchor orbit windows to the session's initial instant rather than the current instant, so playback never triggers regeneration
Regenerate continuously on the same cadence as the state prefetch

questions.question: In scientific mode, are bodies given a minimum on-screen size and a pickable proxy? At 1 AU = 100 scene units with the home view framing Neptune's orbit (~6000 units across), Earth's true-scale mesh radius is 0.0043 units - far below one pixel - so nothing is visible and a pointer raycast against the mesh can essentially never hit it, yet 004 section 18 requires deterministic selection, 004 section 30 requires scientific mode to remain usable, and 006 section 19 requires an E2E test where 'a planet is selected'.

Enforce a minimum rendered mesh radius in pixels (bodies never shrink below ~3 px) in both modes and raycast against the real mesh
Selection in scientific mode happens only via labels or the body list panel; mesh picking is a visualization-mode feature

questions.question: What does POST /api/v1/ephemeris/batch return when part of the request is invalid or fails? Concretely: if one instant in the list falls outside 1900-2100, is the whole request rejected 422, or is that column returned as an error entry? options: Fail fast: any out-of-range instant or unknown body rejects the whole request (422/400) before computation, and a convergence failure mid-batch returns 500 for the whole request

Validate the whole request up front (422/400 on bad input) but tolerate per-pair computation failures: columnar arrays carry null at that index plus a top-level 'errors' array naming (body, instantIndex, code)

questions.question: What exactly happens to the camera on selection and on reference-frame switch? 001 section 3.6 says clicking a body must select it and 'optionally animate the camera toward it' without saying who decides; 004 section 16 requires transitions to be 'smooth, interruptible... safe when changing reference frames' with no duration, no settle distance, and no defined frame-switch behaviour. options: Click selects only; focus is a separate explicit action (double-click or panel button); focus settles at 6x the body's current display radius clamped to the zoom bounds; 800 ms ease-in-out; frame switch keeps the body focused and re-derives its scene position
Click selects and immediately animates focus; same settle/duration rules; frame switch resets to home view and clears tracking
Click selects and focuses only when tracking mode is already on; frame switch preserves camera world position and lets the scene move under it
Focus settles at a fixed per-body distance taken from the presentation registry rather than a multiple of display radius

questions.question: What does the web app do when the API is unavailable, slow, or returns an error? With every celestial state now coming over HTTP, this is on the critical path for initial load, date jumps, playback prefetch and orbit generation, yet no document specifies loading states, retry policy, timeouts, or degraded behaviour. Does playback pause and surface a banner when a prefetch fails? Are failed requests retried - how many times, with what backoff and timeout? If the initial load fails, does the app show an empty scene, the last known state, or an error screen?

options: Fail loud and pause: any prefetch failure pauses the simulation clock and shows a dismissible banner naming the error code; 3 retries with exponential backoff, 10 s timeout; initial-load failure shows a full-screen error with retry
Fail soft: keep rendering the last known state, retry silently in the background, surface an error only after N consecutive failures
No retries in V1 - surface the structured API error immediately and require a manual retry
Local/self-hosted only, so treat failures as developer errors: log to console, no user-facing UI

questions.question: How is simulation time advanced and represented, so that ADR-017's 'deterministic simulation clock' is actually testable? If each frame does instant += playbackRate * frameDelta, the resulting instant depends on frame rate and dropped frames, so the E2E 'time advances / time reverses' scenarios can only assert loose ranges. Is the clock instead anchorInstant + playbackRate * (elapsed since anchor) with an injectable time source for tests? And is simulation time stored as a Julian Date double, epoch milliseconds, or anchor-plus-offset?

options: Anchor-based: clock = anchorInstant + playbackRate * (now - anchorRealTime), re-anchored on every rate/direction/jump change, with an injectable time source so tests advance it deterministically
Fixed-step accumulator decoupled from frame delta - deterministic given the same number of steps
Per-frame accumulation on real frame delta; tests assert ranges rather than exact instants
Anchor-based, with the instant carried as epoch milliseconds and converted to JD only at the API boundary

questions.question: Does the V1 Sun/Earth model (SCHLYTER_SUN_EARTH_V1) produce the position of Earth's centre or of the Earth-Moon barycentre, and is an EMB-to-geocentre correction applied using the lunar model before geocentric subtraction? Schlyter's apparent solar orbit is a low-precision solar theory whose origin convention is not stated in our documents, while the accepted Horizons configuration validates against Earth's body centre (500@399). The offset is ~4670 km (3.1e-5 AU), which is ~24 arcsec of direction error for a body at 0.27 AU (Venus near inferior conjunction) and ~4 arcsec for Mars at opposition.
questions.why_it_matters: It is a systematic error of up to a few tens of arcseconds against a 1-2 arcminute budget, and it will show up as a body-dependent bias in the very validation run that freezes the tolerances — so if it is not decided up front, the frozen baselines silently absorb it. It also decides whether the planetary pipeline has a dependency on the lunar model.
options: Treat the model output as Earth's centre, apply no correction, and document the EMB ambiguity as a known limitation quantified in the validation report
Apply the EMB-to-geocentre correction using SCHLYTER_MOON_V1 (Earth = EMB - Moon*mu) so geocentric states are true geocentric
Validate against the Earth-Moon barycentre (500@3) instead, and document that V1 geocentric means EMB-centric
Decide empirically in the first validation run: measure the residual, then pick

questions.question: For the body that sits at the frame origin (SUN in HELIOCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC, EARTH in GEOCENTRIC_*), the accepted rule returns an exact zero vector. What do the per-body spherical coordinates and distance contain in that case? Longitude/latitude and RA/Dec are mathematically undefined for a zero vector, JSON cannot carry NaN, and the accepted payload contract says every body entry carries 'spherical coordinates appropriate to the requested frame'. Is the sphericalCoordinates object omitted, present with nulls, or present with zeros?
questions.why_it_matters: It changes the Zod/JSON schema (optional vs nullable vs required), the response-schema test in 003 section 21, and what the body-info panel renders for the origin body. A silent choice of 'zeros' also produces a fake RA of 0h that looks like real data.
questions.source: 003 section 8; Round 1 answer `body_frame_matrix`; Round 4 answer `spherical_coordinate_units_and_fields`; 006 section 10 on near-zero quantities.
options: Omit sphericalCoordinates entirely for the origin body; distance is {value: 0, unit: 'AU'}
Include sphericalCoordinates with null angle values and radius 0 (schema fields nullable)
Include zeros for all angles and document that they are meaningless for the origin body
Return an explicit marker, e.g. sphericalCoordinates: { degenerate: true }

questions.question: Is application state (instant, frame, selected body, rendering mode, playback state) reflected in the URL as a deep link, and how do the Playwright E2E scenarios pin a deterministic instant given the accepted default of 'current browser time'? 006 section 19 requires tests for 'default solar system appears', 'date changes' and 'planet is selected', but a wall-clock default makes the initial scene different on every run, and nothing states whether E2E runs against the real Express API or a fixture-backed stub.
questions.why_it_matters: It decides whether the app needs URL-state plumbing at all (a user-facing feature nobody has scoped), how E2E assertions are written, and whether CI must boot the API and astronomy engine for the E2E stage. Retrofitting URL state after the state layer is built is expensive.
options: Full URL state (query params for instant/frame/body/mode) — E2E navigates to a pinned URL and hits the real API
No URL state in V1; E2E injects a fixed instant via the injectable time source already accepted for the simulation clock, against the real API
No URL state; E2E runs against a fixture-backed stub API for full determinism, with a separate smoke test against the real API
URL state for instant and frame only (shareable views), plus the injectable time source for tests

questions.question: How are body labels implemented and what is the occlusion strategy? 004 section 19 requires labels to support 'visibility toggle, distance-based scaling, occlusion strategy, selection emphasis' but never says whether they are DOM elements overlaid on the canvas (e.g. drei Html / CSS2DRenderer) or in-scene sprites, and never defines what 'occlusion' means here — hiding a label whose body is behind another body, hiding labels for off-screen bodies, or de-cluttering overlapping labels.
questions.why_it_matters: DOM labels are queryable by Playwright and accessible to screen readers but cost a reflow per frame; sprite labels are cheap but invisible to the E2E suite, which must then assert label state some other way. The occlusion definition also determines whether per-frame raycasts against every body are needed.
questions.source: 004 section 19; Round 2 answers `renderer_package_ownership` and `default_app_state` (labels on by default); 006 section 19.
options: DOM overlay via drei Html, occlusion = hide when the body is behind another body (drei occlude), plus simple overlap de-cluttering
DOM overlay, no geometric occlusion in V1 — labels always visible for visible bodies, de-cluttered by screen distance only
In-scene sprites with depth testing (natural occlusion); E2E asserts label state via the React state layer rather than the DOM
DOM overlay with distance-based fade only; defer occlusion and de-cluttering to a later milestone

questions.question: Are bodies lit by the Sun light object — showing a terminator and phases (a crescent Venus or Moon in geocentric view) — or rendered fully bright/unlit in V1? And are shadow maps enabled, i.e. can Earth cast a shadow on the Moon or Jupiter's moons? 004 section 10 requires a separate light object and section 11 says 'V1 can use simple materials', which does not resolve lit vs unlit.
questions.why_it_matters: Phase rendering is the most visible science-adjacent behaviour in the geocentric view, and it is also misleading in visualization mode where radii are exaggerated 50x. Shadows are a real performance and correctness decision (eclipse geometry at exaggerated radii is wrong by construction), and retrofitting a material change touches every body renderer.
options: Lit with MeshStandardMaterial from the Sun point light (phases visible), no shadow maps in V1
Lit with phases, and shadow maps enabled only in scientific mode where radii are true
Unlit/fullbright materials in V1; lighting and phases deferred to Milestone 8
Lit, with a documented note in the UI that phases are geometrically distorted in visualization mode

questions.question: What is the 'timeline' deliverable in Milestone 9? Nothing defines its span (the whole 1900-2100 range, or a zoomable window around the current instant), its granularity, whether dragging the scrub handle issues a request per drag position or only on release, or whether it displays anything besides the current instant (e.g. event markers for conjunctions/oppositions, which 006 section 12 mentions only as test dates).
questions.why_it_matters: A 200-year scrubber at one-pixel-per-position is a ~73,000-day range: without a defined zoom/granularity model the control is unusable for picking a specific day, and without a defined drag policy it can fire hundreds of ephemeris requests per drag.
options: Simple full-range scrubber (1900-2100) plus a date-picker input for precision; requests fire on release only
Zoomable timeline with selectable span (year/decade/century) centred on the current instant; requests on release
No scrubber in V1 — date picker plus play/pause/rate/step controls only; timeline deferred
Full-range scrubber with live preview during drag at a throttled request rate

questions.question: What licence does the repository itself carry? 001 section 6 places a LICENSE file at the root and 007 calls this an open-source portfolio project, but no licence is ever named — and the accepted asset choice (Solar System Scope maps, CC-BY) imposes attribution obligations that need somewhere to live.
questions.why_it_matters: An agent creating H001's repository foundation must write a LICENSE file, and the choice affects how Schlyter-derived equations and CC-BY textures may be redistributed. Changing it after public release requires the consent of every contributor.
options: MIT for code, with CC-BY asset attributions recorded in THIRD_PARTY_ASSETS
Apache-2.0 for code (explicit patent grant), CC-BY assets attributed separately
MIT for code and CC-BY-4.0 for docs/validation reports
No licence file in V1 (all rights reserved) until public release is decided

payload.assessment: After five Q&A rounds the specification is unusually complete: the compute location, frame conventions, date range, error taxonomy, model IDs, scene scale, camera behaviour and clock semantics are all now pinned, and most of what remains is second-order. The weakest remaining areas are (a) the playback/prefetch numbers, where the accepted answers still contain placeholders and one internally inconsistent figure (the ~1.5-day sample cap ignores the Moon), (b) the validation layer, where the fixture sampling grid that the empirically frozen tolerances will be derived from is never defined, and (c) the frontend presentation/plumbing details that no document has ever touched — label implementation, lighting, the timeline widget, URL state and E2E determinism. Nothing here blocks the astronomy math tasks (H002–H015); the blocking items land on H020–H022 and the validation tasks.

answers.question: The accepted interpolation rule caps sample spacing so 'the fastest visible body gets >= 60 samples per orbit (~1.5 days)', but 1.5 days is Mercury's figure (88 d / 60). The Moon is a V1 body with a 27.3-day period, which would demand ~0.45-day spacing — a 3.3x higher state rate — and its apparent geocentric motion (~13 deg/day) is the fastest thing on screen. Does the cap apply to the Moon (0.45 d) or only to heliocentric planets (1.5 d), and if the latter, how is the Moon animated between samples?
answers.answer: Cap applies to all bodies including the Moon: 0.45-day spacing globally

answers.question: The accepted prefetch answer still contains placeholders: 'a rolling window via the batch endpoint (state window length in simulation time and number of instants) ... re-fetches when the window is N% consumed', and Round 5 added 'a hard playbackRate cap where that would exceed the 500-instant batch limit' without a number. What are the concrete values for window length (or instants per window), the re-fetch threshold N, the request timeout budget relative to window duration, and the maximum playbackRate? Related: does the earlier 10 Hz recompute cadence still govern at slow playback rates, or is spacing now purely min(playbackRate/10, cap)? And which of the 001 section 45 presets (1 s/s, 1 min/s, 1 hr/s, 1 day/s, 1 month/s, 1 year/s) survive the cap?
